proof.criterion: Reviewer items 4 and the architect's weight-bearing one: the two failures of the reachability step are different, and the loop separates them — a role meeting a refusal is not handed the timeout's reading.

proof.command: a script lifting the `python3 - <host> <port> <<'PY' … PY` body out of the section ; then (1) that body against a local port with a listener started twelve seconds in, (2) against a local port with no listener at all, (3) against the address of a Job I submitted without the reachability label, after `kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready` and with its log showing Postgres `ready to accept connections`
proof.observed: The split holds, and each state reports itself: (1) the loop rides out the refusals and prints `answered`, exit 0, after twelve seconds — the starting-up reading, and proof the loop is what makes a refusal survivable; (2) refusals for the whole minute end `never answered: ConnectionRefusedError: [Errno 111] Connection refused`, exit 1 at 60 s; (3) a workload up and unreachable ends `never answered: TimeoutError: timed out`, exit 1 at 61 s — which is exactly the sentence the section assigns to the missing label, and is distinguishable from (2) by the exception class the step prints. A role meeting a refusal is not handed the timeout's reading in any of the three.
proof.negativeControl: State (3) is the negative control for the label bullet as well: the section's own diagnostic, `kubectl get pod -l job-name=<workload> -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.labels}'`, printed a label set carrying only the Job controller's and the cluster's topology labels, so a role comparing it with the declaration sees the opt-in label is absent. Both Jobs were bounded at a fifteen-minute deadline and a five-minute ttl and deleted by hand.

observations: A third outcome of the reachability step has no reading, and it is adjacent to item 4 rather than one of the eight, so it is recorded here for the architect to route rather than asked for: a connection *refused* for the whole minute ends `never answered: ConnectionRefusedError`, which is a workload reachable but never listening — a server that crashed on its configuration, or the wrong port — and the paragraph reads a refusal as starting up and a timeout as the label. The exception class the step prints is what tells a careful reader, so nothing misleads; a clause would make it explicit.

One claim of the section I could not test and do not dispute: that `postgres:16`'s entrypoint holds its listener closed through initialisation, which is the reviewer's reason for the loop. A workload in that namespace is unreachable from a role container before the declarations are applied, so the first seconds cannot be observed from here; the loop makes the question moot either way, since a refusal is ridden out and a timeout is not.
